subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which post did Stalin hold from 1922 that gave him control over party appointments and membership?
options: General Secretary of the Communist Party
questions.explain: As General Secretary from 1922, Stalin controlled appointments and built a base of loyal supporters.

questions.q: In which year did Lenin die, opening the leadership struggle?
questions.explain: Lenin died in January 1924, triggering the contest to succeed him.

questions.q: Who was Stalin's chief rival, the former Commissar for War who had led the Red Army?
questions.explain: Trotsky, organiser of the Red Army, was seen as Stalin's most dangerous rival.

questions.q: What was the name of Trotsky's policy that Stalin opposed with 'Socialism in One Country'?
questions.explain: Trotsky argued for spreading revolution abroad, while Stalin's 'Socialism in One Country' appealed more to party members.

questions.q: Why did Lenin's Testament pose a threat to Stalin?
options: It named Trotsky as Lenin's chosen successor
It criticised Stalin and suggested he be removed as General Secretary
It banned Stalin from the Politburo
questions.explain: Lenin's Testament warned that Stalin was too rude and had concentrated too much power, recommending his removal.

questions.q: Why did 'Socialism in One Country' help Stalin defeat his rivals?
options: It appealed to party members as realistic and patriotic after years of turmoil
questions.explain: The idea of building socialism within the USSR seemed more achievable and patriotic than Trotsky's global vision.

questions.q: How did Stalin use his early alliance with Zinoviev and Kamenev?
options: To isolate and remove Trotsky from power first
To restore the New Economic Policy permanently
To hand power to the peasants
questions.explain: Stalin joined Zinoviev and Kamenev to sideline Trotsky, then later turned against them too.

questions.q: What was a 'kolkhoz'?
questions.explain: A kolkhoz was a collective farm where peasants pooled land, tools and labour.

questions.q: What term described the wealthier peasants targeted for elimination during collectivisation?
questions.explain: Kulaks, the better-off peasants, were 'liquidated as a class' through dekulakisation.

questions.q: The First Five-Year Plan (1928-1932) concentrated mainly on which sector?
options: Heavy industry such as coal, iron and steel
questions.explain: The First Five-Year Plan prioritised heavy industry to modernise and strengthen the USSR.

questions.q: Which body was responsible for setting the targets of the Five-Year Plans?
questions.explain: Gosplan, the state planning agency, drew up and set the production targets.

questions.q: Who was Alexei Stakhanov, who gave his name to a movement in 1935?
options: A coal miner celebrated for record output
The head of the secret police
questions.explain: Stakhanov reportedly mined a huge quantity of coal in one shift, inspiring the Stakhanovite movement to boost productivity.

questions.q: Why did Stalin want to collectivise agriculture?
options: To give peasants private ownership of large estates
To increase grain output and fund industrialisation while extending state control over the countryside
To reduce the size of the Red Army
questions.explain: Collectivisation aimed to raise grain production, feed cities, earn export income for industry and control the peasantry.

questions.q: What was a major consequence of collectivisation in 1932-33?
options: A severe famine, worst in Ukraine, killing millions
A rapid rise in peasant living standards
The abolition of the Communist Party
questions.explain: Disruption, grain requisitioning and resistance produced a devastating famine, especially in Ukraine.

questions.q: Why were the Five-Year Plan targets often unrealistic?
options: They were set deliberately low to guarantee success
They were extremely high to force rapid industrial growth, encouraging exaggerated or falsified figures
They were chosen by foreign advisers
questions.explain: Punishing targets drove huge growth but also led managers to exaggerate or fake results to avoid punishment.

questions.q: Whose murder in December 1934 was used by Stalin as a pretext to launch the purges?
questions.explain: The assassination of the popular Leningrad leader Kirov gave Stalin an excuse to begin mass arrests.

questions.q: What was the NKVD?
questions.explain: The NKVD was the secret police that carried out arrests, executions and ran the Gulag.

questions.q: What were the public 'show trials' of 1936-1938?
options: Staged trials where leading Communists confessed to invented crimes
questions.explain: In the Moscow show trials, Old Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin confessed to fabricated charges.

questions.q: Why did the purge of the Red Army officers weaken the USSR?
options: It removed experienced commanders such as Marshal Tukhachevsky, damaging military leadership
It increased the number of trained generals
It gave the army new modern weapons
questions.explain: Executing thousands of officers, including Tukhachevsky in 1937, stripped the army of experienced leadership.

questions.q: How did Stalin use propaganda and the 'cult of personality'?
options: To present himself as an all-wise, heroic leader through posters, art and rewritten history
To encourage free criticism of the government
To reduce his own public image
questions.explain: Socialist Realist art, posters, films and rewritten history glorified Stalin as an infallible leader.

questions.q: In 1930 a peasant kills his livestock and burns his grain rather than hand them to the new collective farm. This action best illustrates:
questions.explain: Many peasants destroyed crops and animals as a protest against being forced into collective farms.

questions.q: A historian finds a 1939 photograph that has been edited to erase an official executed in the purges. This is an example of:
options: The use of propaganda to rewrite history
questions.explain: The regime doctored photographs and texts to erase purged figures from the historical record.

questions.q: At a 1936 Moscow trial an Old Bolshevik confesses in public to crimes he clearly did not commit. What best explains this?
options: Confessions were extracted through torture, threats to family and intimidation
The trial was a fair legal process
questions.explain: NKVD pressure, torture and threats against relatives forced defendants to confess in the show trials.

questions.q: A factory manager in 1932 reports meeting his steel target, though real output was far lower. Which feature of the Five-Year Plans does this show?
options: Falsification of figures caused by pressure to meet unrealistic targets
The success of the New Economic Policy
questions.explain: Fear of punishment for missing impossible targets led managers to exaggerate or falsify production figures.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE History (4HI1) specification; The USSR under Stalin 1924-53
